projects.title: To-Do List App
projects.tagline: The classic first app: add, tick off, filter and save your tasks.
desc: You'll build a complete to-do app from an empty file: an HTML form, CSS that makes it look like an app, and JavaScript that handles adding, completing, deleting and filtering, with everything saved in the browser.
Along the way you'll learn the pattern behind React, Vue and every other framework: keep your data in an array, and re-draw the page from it whenever it changes.
projects.final: A to-do app that adds tasks with Enter, ticks them off, deletes them, filters by status, counts what's left and remembers everything after a refresh.
projects.prereq: the **Build Your First Web Page** bootcamp course, or knowing what HTML tags and CSS rules are.
stretch: Double-click a to-do to edit its text.
Add a **Clear completed** button.
Add due dates and sort by them.
Drag to reorder (the HTML Drag and Drop API).

milestones.goal: Structure and style: a form and a list that look like an app.

body: Every web app starts as HTML: the structure your JavaScript will bring to life later. A `<form>` groups an input with its button, and it gives you a single **submit** event whether people click **Add** or press Enter.

steps.title: Listen for the form
body: JavaScript makes the page react. First, find the elements with `document.querySelector`, then **listen** for events with `addEventListener`.

By default, submitting a form reloads the page, which would wipe your app. `event.preventDefault()` stops that. `console.log` prints to the console under the preview, which is your best debugging friend.

milestones.title: Done and delete
milestones.goal: Move the data into an array and render from it.

steps.title: Keep the data in an array
body: So far the page *is* the data. That gets messy once items can change. The fix every framework uses: keep the data in a JavaScript array (the **state**) and write one `render()` function that rebuilds the list from it.
Each to-do becomes an object, `{ id, text, done }`. Changing the app is then always the same two moves: update the array, call `render()`.
steps.task: Add `let todos = [];`. Make `addTodo` push `{ id, text, done: false }` and call `render()`. Write `render()` to clear `#list` and add one `li` (containing a `span` with the text) per to-do.

steps.title: Tick things off
body: Each item gets a checkbox. When it changes, flip that to-do's `done` flag and re-render. `array.find(t => t.id === id)` returns the first item matching a condition.

steps.title: Delete items
body: `array.filter(...)` returns a new array with only the items that pass the test. To delete, keep everything **except** the one with that id: `todos = todos.filter(t => t.id !== id)`.
That's why `todos` is declared with `let`: you replace it with the filtered array.

steps.title: Count what's left
body: A count of unfinished items is **derived state**: never store it, compute it inside `render()` from the array, so it can never be wrong.
Grammar matters: `1 item left` but `2 items left`. A ternary `left === 1 ? "item" : "items"` handles it.

milestones.goal: Filter by status and remember everything between visits.

steps.title: Filters: all, active, done
body: A filter is just one more piece of state: `let filter = "all"`. `render()` shows only the to-dos that match it.

steps.title: Save to localStorage
body: Refresh the page and everything's gone. `localStorage` keeps strings in the browser between visits. Arrays aren't strings, so convert with `JSON.stringify(todos)` when saving.
Since every change already goes through `render()`, saving there means you can never forget to save.

projects.title: Calculator
projects.tagline: A real calculator with chaining, decimals, keyboard support and no floating-point surprises.
desc: You'll build a working calculator, the kind that's on every phone, from a grid of buttons to correct maths. It's a perfect first lesson in **state**: what the program has to remember between clicks.
You'll also meet real-world edge cases that tutorials skip: double decimal points, chained operations, dividing by zero and why `0.1 + 0.2` isn't `0.3`.

steps.title: Floating point and dividing by zero
body: Try `0.1 + 0.2`: JavaScript says `0.30000000000000004`. Computers store decimals in binary, which can't represent 0.1 exactly. The fix for display is rounding: `Number(n.toFixed(10))` gives `0.3`.

projects.title: Number Guessing Game
projects.tagline: Your first complete Python game: random numbers, loops, input and a best score.
desc: The perfect first Python project. You'll go from one line to a polished little game, meeting variables, functions, `while` loops, user input, error handling and refactoring along the way.
Every concept arrives exactly when the game needs it, so it sticks.
projects.final: A command-line game that picks a secret number, tells you whether each guess is too high or too low, survives typos, rates your skill and keeps your best score across rounds.
projects.prereq: the first half of **Python from Zero** (print, variables, if).
stretch: Add difficulty levels (1–10, 1–100, 1–1000) with a guess limit.
Make the computer guess *your* number using binary search.
Save the best score to a file with `open()`.

milestones.title: The rules
milestones.goal: A secret number and a function that judges guesses.

steps.title: Pick a secret number
body: Python comes with a library of ready-made tools. `import random` loads the module for random numbers, and `random.randint(1, 100)` returns a whole number from 1 to 100, **including** both ends.
Store it in a variable so the rest of the program can compare guesses against it.

steps.title: Judge a guess
body: Put the rule of the game in a **function**: given the secret and a guess, return `"Too low"`, `"Too high"` or `"Correct"`. A function with no printing and no input is easy to test and reuse.
Each `return` ends the function immediately, so you don't need `elif` after a branch that returns.
steps.task: Write `check_guess(secret, guess)` returning `"Too low"`, `"Too high"` or `"Correct"`.

milestones.title: The game loop
milestones.goal: Read guesses until the player wins, without crashing on typos.

steps.title: Keep guessing until it's right
body: `input("Your guess: ")` waits for the player to type a line and returns it as a **string**. `int(...)` turns it into a number you can compare.
`while True:` repeats forever; `break` jumps out once the guess is correct. Count the attempts as you go.
In this editor, `input()` reads from the **Input** box above the editor: one line per call. The checks fill it in for you.
steps.task: Write a `while True` loop that reads a guess with `input`, converts it with `int`, counts `attempts`, prints the result of `check_guess`, and stops when it's correct. Afterwards print `You got it in N attempts.`
steps.solution:
import random


def check_guess(secret, guess):
    if guess < secret:
        return "Too low"
    if guess > secret:
        return "Too high"
    return "Correct"


secret = random.randint(1, 100)
print("I'm thinking of a number between 1 and 100.")

attempts = 0
while True:
    guess = int(input("Your guess: "))
    attempts += 1
    result = check_guess(secret, guess)
    print(result)
    if result == "Correct":
        break
print(f"You got it in {attempts} attempts.")

`attempts` counts every guess (the checks guess 1, 2, 3 and so on).
You use a `while` loop.

steps.title: Survive bad input
body: Type `abc` and `int("abc")` crashes the program with a `ValueError`. Real programs expect bad input and recover.
`try:` runs code that might fail; `except ValueError:` runs only if that error happens. `continue` skips straight to the next loop round without counting the attempt.
steps.task: Wrap the conversion in `try`/`except ValueError`. On bad input print `Please enter a whole number.` and `continue` without counting an attempt.

milestones.title: A proper game
milestones.goal: Clean functions, a rating and replays with a best score.

steps.title: Refactor into a function

projects.title: Password Toolkit
projects.tagline: Score passwords, explain how to fix them, block common ones and generate strong replacements.
desc: You'll build the kind of password checker you see on sign-up forms, plus a generator, and learn why some approaches are secure and others aren't.
It's a compact tour of strings, booleans, `any`/`all`, sets and the standard library, with a real security lesson attached.

steps.title: The length rule
body: Length is the single biggest factor in password strength: every extra character multiplies the guesses an attacker needs.
A function that answers a yes/no question returns a **boolean**. `len(password) >= 8` already *is* `True` or `False`, so return it directly instead of writing an `if`.

steps.title: A strength score
body: Score a password out of 6: one point each for 8+ characters, 12+ characters, a lowercase letter, an uppercase letter, a digit and a symbol.
`any(c.isupper() for c in password)` asks *is there at least one uppercase character?* String methods like `isupper`, `isdigit` and `isalnum` (letter or digit) do the per-character test.

projects.title: Bank Account System
projects.tagline: Object-oriented Python done properly: classes, rules, custom exceptions and inheritance.
desc: Banking is the classic way to learn object-oriented programming because the rules are clear and mistakes are obvious: money must never appear or vanish.

projects.title: Tic-Tac-Toe with an Unbeatable AI
projects.tagline: Write the minimax algorithm and build an opponent that never loses.
desc: The game is simple; the AI is the lesson. You'll implement **minimax**, the recursive search behind classic game-playing programs, and watch it play perfectly.
Along the way: board representation, list comprehensions, recursion with backtracking, and testing an algorithm against scripted opponents before a human ever touches it.

steps.title: Draw the board

steps.title: Who won?
body: There are only 8 winning lines: 3 rows, 3 columns, 2 diagonals. List them as tuples of indexes and check each one.
Python allows chained comparisons: `board[a] == board[b] == board[c]` means both equalities hold. Remember to ignore three *empty* squares in a row.

steps.title: Minimax: looking ahead
body: How does a computer play perfectly? It imagines **every** possible future. **Minimax** scores a finished game +1 if X won, −1 if O won and 0 for a draw. X picks the move with the highest score, O the lowest, assuming both play perfectly.
It's **recursion**: to score a position, try each move, score the resulting position with `minimax` itself, then undo the move. Base cases are finished games.
steps.task: Write `minimax(board, player)` returning +1, −1 or 0: the result with perfect play from here, where `player` moves next. Try each free square, recurse with the other player, undo the move, and return the max (X) or min (O).

steps.title: Escape HTML first
body: Markdown is text people write; HTML is what browsers run. If someone types `<script>`, it must appear as text, never as code. Escaping replaces `&`, `<` and `>` with **entities**: `&`, `<` and `>`.
Order matters: replace `&` first. Otherwise the `&` inside a freshly made `<` would be escaped again.

steps.title: The most common words
body: `counts.items()` gives `(word, count)` pairs. Sort them with a **key function**: `lambda pair: (-pair[1], pair[0])` sorts by count, biggest first (the minus sign), and alphabetically when counts tie.

steps.solution:
import string

TEXT = """Coding is a craft. You learn it by writing code, reading code and fixing code.
The best way to learn is to build small things, then bigger things.
Every bug you fix teaches you something. Every project you finish makes the next one easier.
So write a little code every day, and be patient with yourself."""


def words(text):
    result = []
    for raw in text.split():
        word = raw.strip(string.punctuation).lower()
        if word:
            result.append(word)
    return result


def frequencies(text):
    counts = {}
    for word in words(text):
        counts[word] = counts.get(word, 0) + 1
    return counts


def top_words(text, n):
    counts = frequencies(text)
    ranked = sorted(counts.items(), key=lambda pair: (-pair[1], pair[0]))
    return ranked[:n]


print(len(words(TEXT)), "words")
print(len(frequencies(TEXT)), "different words")
print(top_words(TEXT, 5))

desc: Every online shop runs the same logic underneath the pretty pages. You'll write it as small, testable functions: no HTML, just the rules.

steps.title: Products and prices in cents
body: Money and floating point don't mix: `0.1 + 0.2` is `0.30000000000000004`. Shops store prices as whole **cents** and only convert to dollars for display.
An object keyed by product id is a quick lookup table: `PRODUCTS.mug.price` is `950`.

steps.title: Add to cart, without mutating
body: A cart is an array of lines like `{ id: "mug", qty: 2 }`. Instead of changing it, return a **new** array: `[...cart, line]` copies and appends, and `map` with `{ ...line, qty }` copies one line with a new quantity.
Never changing data in place (**immutability**) is how React and Redux work, and it makes bugs much easier to find. Throwing an `Error` for an unknown id catches typos early.

steps.title: Shuffle fairly
body: The **Fisher–Yates shuffle** walks from the end of the array, swapping each item with a random one at or before it. Every order is equally likely, unlike the popular `sort(() => Math.random() - 0.5)`, which is biased.
